description: We are Team CarettaCarettas, a group of friends who love solving problems and building new things. We are excited to work together and create a great project at this challenge!
summary: Caretta Health is an offline-first health companion designed for astronauts operating far from Earth. During deep-space missions communication delays can reach up to 24 light-minutes one way, requiring crews without formal medical training to independently monitor their health against NASA's five human spaceflight hazards. Caretta empowers astronauts through a four-step loop: measure, understand, act, and escalate. Users track 10 key health indicators using a color-blind-friendly traffic-light system. The platform combines an interactive 3D space-health body map, a triage tool for 44 space conditions, and an engine tracking gradual physiological shifts. Thresholds and guidance dynamically adapt across five environments, from the space station to lunar and Martian bases. Built with Python, FastAPI, SQLite, and Streamlit, Caretta operates with zero cloud dependencies and 87 passing tests, ready to support both future space crews and remote clinics on Earth.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
Caretta is a web app that helps astronauts check their own health during space missions. The name comes from the loggerhead sea turtle (Caretta caretta), which carries its home across the oceans. In the same way, astronauts carry Caretta far from Earth.

The app works in four steps: measure, understand, act, and ask for help when needed.

  • Daily check-in: The astronaut enters up to 10 health values: heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen level (SpO₂), body temperature, blood sugar, sleep, mood, exercise time, and radiation dose. They can also add photos.
  • Interactive body map: A human figure made of thousands of moving particles. When you click a body system (heart, lungs, brain, bones, and others), the particles form that organ. The app then shows how space affects it, the latest values, and what to do.
  • “How are you feeling?” triage: The app asks simple questions one at a time, starting with emergency signs. It ends with one of 44 space-related results. Each result comes with how urgent it is, what to do, and who to involve.
  • Trends: Charts and a mission calendar show changes over time. The app pays more attention to repeated problems than to one bad reading.
  • Care team page: The flight surgeon sees which crew members need attention and why, and can download a short health report with one click.

What are the benefits?

  • Astronauts can understand their own health without medical training.
  • They get clear, simple actions, and they know when to call the crew medical officer or the flight surgeon.
  • It works offline. Crews going to Mars cannot always talk to Earth, because messages can take up to 24 light-minutes.
  • Doctors on Earth get short, useful reports instead of raw data.

What is the intended impact?
We want to help astronauts stay healthy and safe on long missions to the Moon and Mars, where help from Earth is slow or not possible. The same idea can also help people in other remote places, such as Antarctic stations, submarines, ships, or rural areas far from doctors.

What tools did we use?

  • Language: Python
  • Web app: Streamlit
  • API: FastAPI, so wearables and other devices can send data to the app
  • Database: SQLite
  • Data and charts: pandas, NumPy, and Plotly
  • Images: Pillow
  • Body map: HTML Canvas and JavaScript (our own particle animation)
  • Code and hosting: GitHub and Streamlit Community Cloud
  • AI Tool: ClaudeCode

How is our project creative?

  • The animated particle body map turns health data into something visual and easy to explore.
  • The app adapts to five environments: space station, deep-space travel, Moon base, Mars base, and rover. Each has its own limits, risks, and advice. For example, the communication delay on Mars changes when and how to contact the ground team.
  • The triage questions are built for space problems, not only for normal problems on Earth.
  • Mission patches and streaks make health checks feel like part of the mission, not extra work.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Science: The app is based on NASA’s Human Research Program and the five hazards of spaceflight: radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, gravity changes, and a hostile environment.
  • Simple language: We avoided medical terms where we could, because users may not have medical knowledge.
  • Accessibility: Colors always come with shapes and words, and the body map has a list option for keyboard users.
  • Offline use: All data is stored on the device, with no need for the internet.
  • Safety: The app supports decisions but does not replace doctors. It always tells users when to contact the flight surgeon. Caretta is a prototype for education and decision support, not a medical device.

GitHub: https://github.com/mertckoglu/caretta-health.git
